UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                      BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                          )
Midcontinent Independent System                           )                        Docket No. ER26-3650-000
   Operator, Inc.                                         )

                        NOTICE OF INTERVENTION AND COMMENTS OF
                          THE ORGANIZATION OF MISO STATES, INC.

           The Organization of MISO States, Inc. (“OMS”) submits this Notice of Intervention and

Comments regarding proposed tariff revisions filed by the Midcontinent Independent System

Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) in the

above-captioned proceeding.1 On August 28, 2026, MISO filed proposed revisions to its Open

Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserves Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish

certain Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads (“IRR Filing”). As noted in its

transmittal letter, MISO’s IRR Filing includes a new Section 37A of the Tariff and proposes

requirements that directly address several aspects of the Commission’s directives in its Show

Cause Order issued on June 18, 2026.2 Specifically, MISO proposes visibility, ramp rate, and

disturbance ride-through requirements for Large Loads, as well as transition provisions designed

to minimize disruption to existing commercial arrangements.

     I.    NOTICE OF INTERVENTION

           OMS is a non-profit, self-governing organization comprising representatives from the

seventeen regulatory bodies with jurisdiction over entities participating in MISO and serves as the

    II.    COMMENTS

           OMS supports stringent and clear Tariff requirements needed to address interconnection

reliability and data transparency concerns associated with Large Loads. MISO’s IRR Filing

establishes guidelines and requirements for the integration of Large Loads that will be increasingly

important to the future reliability of the Bulk Electric System (“BES”). With Large Loads

becoming a key driver of increases in interconnection requests and electricity demand growth, this

is an important time to establish appropriate reliability requirements for these resources.

           The IRR Filing is intended to respond to the Commission’s Show Cause Order and appears

to establish important requirements for Large Loads to address system reliability during a period

of dramatic growth in interconnection requests and electricity demand driven primarily by these


3
    18 C.F.R. § 385.214(a)(2) (2026).

                                                 2
 loads. The size of these loads, their speed to power requirements, and the new operational risks

introduced by computational loads warrant a regulatory response to ensure the stability of the BES.

To this end, OMS generally supports MISO’s focus on Visibility, Phasor Measurement Unit

(“PMU”), Ramp, and Ride-Through Requirements, recognizing the potential for improvements as

knowledge is gained on these types of loads. While NERC’s process to develop industry-wide

guidelines is underway, it is appropriate to implement requirements now to safeguard reliability

and complement NERC’s eventual requirements.

           OMS recommends that the Commission evaluate the various proposals for Large Load

requirements before it holistically, recognizing that Large Loads may interconnect across multiple

transmission providers and that consistent, appropriately coordinated requirements will be

important to maintaining BES reliability. Once the various proposals are filed, the Commission

should consider whether additional coordination or standardization is necessary to ensure that

reliability requirements appropriately address the risks presented by Large Loads across the

broader interconnected system. Further, reliability requirements must consider the relative costs

and benefits of any proposals, as well as how those costs will be allocated. OMS is concerned that

MISO’s application fails to address these important issues.

           In the sections below, OMS highlights the importance of each of the proposed requirements

and their importance to the MISO region.

           A.       OMS Generally Supports the New Large Load and Computational Load
                    Definitions and Applicability of the Interconnection Reliability Requirements.

           MISO’s definition of “Large Load”4 in the IRR Filing is generally consistent with an

emerging industry approach that uses a 50 megawatt (“MW”) threshold to identify loads subject


4
    IRR Filing, Tab A (IRR Tariff Redlines) at Definitions – L (“Proposed IRR Tariff”); IRR Filing, Tab C (Prepared
    Direct Testimony of BeiBei Li, Senior Manager of Strategic Assessment) at 12.

                                                           3
 to enhanced reliability requirements.5 While a 50 MW threshold is relatively low compared to the

gigawatt-scale load additions being proposed across the country, it is important to note that MISO

has also included a separate definition of Computational Load. MISO’s separate definition of

Computational Load appropriately recognizes that certain loads present operational characteristics

and reliability risks that warrant additional requirements beyond those applicable to Large Loads

generally. Computational Loads can experience dramatic and coordinated changes in demand,

potentially across multiple facilities, that may create significant impacts to system voltage,

frequency, and stability. Establishing additional requirements for these loads is therefore

appropriate.

          MISO’s IRR Filing establishes requirements applicable to Large Loads and Computational

Loads, identifies the circumstances under which exceptions may apply, and defines the

requirements for those exceptions. OMS supports subjecting all Large Loads to visibility

requirements, with Computational Loads being subject to additional PMU, Ride-Through, and

Ramp requirements to account for their potentially increased operational risks.

          B.      OMS Generally Supports the Transition Provisions.

          OMS generally supports MISO’s proposed transition provisions, which apply the full set

of Interconnection Reliability Requirements to incoming Large Loads while limiting application

of the IRR to Large Loads that are in an advanced stage of development as of December 4, 2026.

These provisions appear to balance the need to avoid disrupting existing commercial arrangements

with the need to ensure that the substantial majority of new Large Loads are subject to meaningful

visibility and reliability requirements.




5
    PJM, SPP, CAISO, ISO-NE, etc.

                                                4
           OMS recognizes the practical and legal considerations associated with applying new

requirements to projects that are already significantly advanced in their development. At the same

time, reliability risks associated with Large Loads do not necessarily depend on when a load

becomes operational. Accordingly, OMS encourages the Commission and MISO to continue to

consider whether the transition provisions appropriately balance these considerations and, in

particular, whether loads that present material reliability risks should be subject to appropriate

reliability requirements regardless of their development status.

          OMS is concerned with MISO’s decision to exempt qualifying Large Loads from Ramp

and Ride-Through requirements for Large Load additions through MTEP 2026. As of the

September 2026 System Planning Committee, MISO has planned for 46.5 GW of Large Load

additions in their Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) process since 2020.6 MISO’s reasoning for

grandfathering this magnitude of Large Loads is unclear to OMS and may constitute a significant

reliability risk to the grid despite the applicability of other visibility requirements to all Large

Loads. The fact that some Large Loads are further along in the development process does not

justify exempting them from these important requirements governing Ramp and Ride-Through

capabilities and procedures that will eventually apply to all future Large Loads.

          C.      OMS Generally Supports MISO’s Proposed Operational Requirements.

          MISO’s proposed Visibility, PMU, Ramp, and Ride-Through Requirements appear to align

with the Commission’s direction in the Show Cause Order and appropriately distinguish between

the reliability risks presented by Large Loads and the risks presented by Computational Loads.

Taken together, MISO intends these requirements to respond to the Commission’s direction to



6
    Preliminary MTEP26 Review, MISO System Planning Committee of the Board (Sept. 15, 2026), available at:
    https://cdn.misoenergy.org/20260915%20System%20Planning%20Committee%20of%20the%20BOD%20Item%2
    005%20Preliminary%20MTEP26%20Review780457.pdf.

                                                      5
 establish a framework for obtaining information and operational capabilities to maintain reliability

as these loads increasingly connect to the BES.

       The Visibility requirements are foundational to this framework and are designed to provide

necessary information about the Large Loads coming onto the system that planners and operators

can use to support assessments and reliability risks based on real data. OMS strongly supports

applying these Visibility requirements to all Large Loads, as MISO has proposed. While MISO

has proposed high-level requirements in its Tariff, OMS recognizes that significant implementation

details will need to be developed in the Business Practice Manuals (“BPMs”). OMS expects to

engage in this process to help ensure that the requirements provide MISO and impacted entities

with the information necessary to plan and operate the system while remaining practical for Load

Serving Entities and Large Load Customers.

       OMS also recognizes that forecasting requirements for Large Loads present unique

challenges. The rapid development of these facilities, uncertainty regarding project timelines and

ultimate load levels, and the potential for substantial deviations between forecasted and actual

demand may make accurate forecasting difficult. OMS encourages the Commission, MISO, and

its stakeholder community to carefully consider the appropriate level of forecasting obligations,

including how responsibility for inaccurate forecasts should be allocated and whether penalties or

other consequences are appropriate when forecasts prove inaccurate despite reasonable efforts to

comply with the requirements.

       It is also appropriate to apply Ramp requirements to Computational Large Loads. Since

these individual loads are often coordinated by a single owner across multiple sites, there is a

significant risk of near-instantaneous, multi-gigawatt ramping needs. Such changes could exceed

the ability of the BES to respond within a given timeframe. Establishing an initial 30 MW/minute



                                                  6
 ramping limit for Large Loads, while providing MISO the ability to authorize deviations based on

the operational capabilities of the BES, appropriately balances reliability considerations with the

operational needs of these loads. This approach will reduce the risk of reliability impacts while

allowing Computational Loads to ramp more rapidly when system conditions permit. The BPM

should include language that decisions to authorize deviations shall be shared among the LSEs that

own the generation, applicable Transmission Owners, and MISO.

       Finally, Ride-Through requirements are necessary for similar reasons. Recent grid events

have demonstrated that the sudden tripping of clusters of Large Loads can create cascading impacts

and place significant strain on the BES. Applying Ride-Through requirements to Computational

Loads is therefore appropriate to mitigate their unique risks, support system stability during

disturbances, and assist with system recovery during stability events. However, MISO Ride-

Through requirements must be market tested; if the inverter market can meet these requirements,

they are appropriate.

 III. CONCLUSION

       OMS submits these Comments because a majority of OMS members support this filing.

This should not be construed to mean that all OMS members agree with all comments herein.

Individual OMS members reserve the right to file separate comments. In recognition of such, the

following members voted in support of this filing:

       Illinois Commerce Commission
       Iowa Utilities Commission
       Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission
